Thanks for having me. I should be careful here, because I don't want to put words in Professor Zhang's mouth or claim details from that conversation more precisely than I can stand behind. So I'll talk about the shift in my own thinking that came out of exchanges like that one.

Coming from a research background, I used to think of machine-learning systems mostly as algorithms plus some engineering to make them run. You design a better attention mechanism or a smarter scheduling policy, write a paper, and the implementation is a detail. Talking with people who have spent years on real systems changed that view. The hard part is often not the core idea. It's everything around it.

The first thing that changed was my sense of what "correct" means. In research code, if your benchmark number goes up, you're happy. In a system that thousands of people depend on, correctness means it works across dozens of hardware configurations, model architectures, and usage patterns, many of which you never imagined. A clever optimization that breaks one edge case can do more harm than good.

The second was the importance of abstraction boundaries. In inference engines especially, models change very fast. Every few months there's a new architecture, a new attention variant, a new quantization format. If your system is built around the assumptions of last year's models, you end up rewriting it constantly. So much of the real engineering challenge is deciding which parts should be general, which should be specialized, and where to draw the line so the system can evolve without collapsing under its own complexity.

The third was the human side. A large open-source system is as much a coordination problem as a technical one: reviewing contributions, maintaining code quality, and keeping the design coherent when many people with different goals are pushing in different directions. That's not something you learn from papers.

So the biggest change for me was respect for engineering as its own discipline, with its own depth, rather than as the thing you do after the research is finished.

fable-5.1.text:
Before that conversation, I honestly thought of systems work as a kind of plumbing. You had a model, you had an algorithm, and the job of the systems person was to make it run fast enough that nobody complained. The interesting part, in my head, was always the algorithm.

Professor Zhang pushed back on that pretty hard. He asked me a simple question: when a training run of a large model fails at step forty thousand, who is responsible for figuring out why? The algorithm person says the loss looked fine. The infrastructure person says the GPUs were healthy. And then the run is dead, and a week of compute is gone. His point was that this gap is not a plumbing problem. It is a design problem, and nobody owns it unless you make someone own it.

That reframed things for me in two ways.

First, I started to see that in machine-learning systems, the engineering difficulty is mostly about the interfaces between layers, not the layers themselves. Communication libraries, memory management, scheduling, the way the framework exposes parallelism. Each of these is well understood in isolation. The hard part is that a decision in one layer silently changes the assumptions of another. He gave examples where a change meant to reduce memory ended up making the collective communication pattern much worse, and nobody noticed for weeks because the metrics each team looked at were all green.

Second, he made me take observability seriously. I used to treat logging and profiling as something you add when things break. He argued that in large-scale training, you cannot reproduce most failures, so if you did not capture the right information the first time, the failure is simply lost. That changed how I write code now. I spend much more effort on making a system explain itself than I used to.

So I would say the change was less about any specific technique and more about where I think the difficulty lives. It is in the boundaries, in the assumptions people make about each other's components, and in whether you can see what the system is actually doing. That is a much more humbling view of the work, but I think it is the correct one.
